summary:
Section 3 of the draft holds on the FreeInference trace, and none of its Fetch candidates (F1, F3) shows a measurable TTFT gain on the campaign 34 logs; campaign 26's trace is the one exception to the falling-hazard claim.

1. Hint shapes (3,787 trees the campaigns draw from, 103,215 gaps). The pooled tool hazard falls from the first second: 0.68, 0.47, 0.28, 0.16, 0.11, 0.058, 0.027, 0.007, 0.002 per s over 0-1, 1-2, 2-4, 4-6, 6-10, 10-20, 20-60, 60-300, 300-1,200 s. The human (no-call) hazard is 0.02-0.04 up to 4 s, flat at 0.007-0.009 from 4 to 60 s, then falls. By key the hazard is highest in the first second for 47 % of returning requests, at 1-2 s for 38 %, at 2 s or later for 15 % (8.5 points are the no-call bump at 2-4 s); F(4|s) rises more than 0.05 above F(4|0) for 4.8 %.
2. Sharpness: p90/p10 by key has median 18.7. The only key under 5 has gaps shorter than a read ("other", 0.51/0.63/1.19 s, 7 % of requests). Keys sharp inside 1-6 s (web_search 2.2/5.6/15.9 s, terminal/ps, the hermes+glm-5-turbo terminal keys) carry about 1-3 %. A stream ends after 22 % of no-call replies and 1.5 % of tool replies.
3. Value before arrival, trace level, c = 1, prefix out of memory at the turn's end: the exact-gap ceiling is 0.80/1.24/1.82/2.25 s per reading request at x = r - W = 1/2/4/6 s. The engine's read_start on the fitted entry nets +0.94/+0.44/+0.04 s (x = 2) and +1.31/+0.80/+0.20 s (x = 4) at lambda = 1e-6/2e-5/1e-4. Nearly all of it is "read now", which is keeping the prefix, plus giving the pin back; a timed start adds at most 0.024 s in sample and nothing out of sample. Six of the twelve (r, W) cells have W >= r and give 0, as does c = 0.
4. For prefixes out of memory 10 s or more the rule nets +0.59/+0.015/+0.002 s (x = 4) of a 3.7 s ceiling. On the runs the ceiling min(gap, stall) per returning request is 0.000-0.017 s in campaign 34's minutes 0-30, at most 0.002 s weighted by c in minutes 30-70, 0.000 in 70-110, and 0.003 s in campaign 33. Campaign 26 (Triton, x10 gaps) differs: its entries are sharp (p90/p10 median 3.7), the ceiling is 0.23-0.29 s, and exact hints took 0.15-0.22 s of it.
5. F1, estimate errors: at arrival the position-over-rate estimate of the GPU turn is unbiased in minutes 30-70 (median 0.0 s, p5/p95 about -4/+5 s) and 9-10 s too long at the median in minutes 90-110, because 51 % of the turns ahead are waiting on their own reads. At the release in minutes 30-70 the error has p5 -3.8 to -2.2 s, p20 -1.4 to -1.1 s, p80 +1.7 to +1.8 s.
6. F1, replay: today's 2 s equals the 20th percentile of that error on held reads in all four arms (+1.6 to +2.1 s). At 2 s, 21-23 % of held reads land late, with 0.8-1.5 s of stall and 64-66K token-seconds pinned per held read. Margin 0 gives 54-55 % late and 28-31K; margin 4 gives 13-15 % late and 111-118K. For ec_full, 2 s is within 1-4 % of the best cost when lambda/c is about 2e-5.
7. No read was held with the pool under 0.90. Where the hold binds, measured c is 0.005-0.06 (minutes 30-70) or 0.000 (70-110). In minutes 30-70 the rule changes the regime's mean TTFT by -0.005 to +0.23 s counted on readers and at most 0.013 s weighted by c, and moves pinned memory from 17.7K tokens to between 1.4K and 31K (about 1 % of the host pool).
8. F3, the line: release to dispatch takes a median 0.0 / 0.09 / 11-12 / 42-44 s in minutes 0-30 / 30-70 / 70-90 / 90-110; dispatch to usable takes 0.4-0.7 / 0.9-1.0 / 2.3-2.5 / 2.8 s. The pre-arrival planner's read time is twice too long with an empty line (2.1 s against 1.1 s) and 2.8 and 7.5 times too short in minutes 70-90 and 90-110 (5.5 against 14.9 s, 6.1 against 46.6 s). The hold's estimate, which counts parked reads ahead by deadline, has a median absolute error of 2.5-3.4 s there.
9. With the true read time and today's c = 1, the expected-cost rule would stage 52 % of the saturated phase's stalled readers (601 reads against 1) for 0.000 s weighted by c, so F3 should not ship without F2.

Not established: lambda was not measured (the range used is inferred); the margin replay is open loop; that a stall second at c = 0 costs the sum nothing is the draft's argument, not tested here. Campaigns 32 and 35 were not used. CPU only; nothing written outside the ev_fetch folder.

findings.question: 1a. Is the gap hazard rising or falling with idle time for the pooled tool and human classes (0-10 s, 10-60 s, beyond), empirically and in the two-piece lognormal the engine fits?
findings.answer:
Falling for the tool class everywhere; falling for the human class except a bump at 2-4 s and a flat stretch from 4 to 60 s.

Replayed population (3,787 trees under --max-context 65536, 103,215 gaps), hazard per s in bins 0-1, 1-2, 2-4, 4-6, 6-10, 10-20, 20-60, 60-300, 300-1,200 s:
- Tool (94,446 gaps, p10/p50/p90 0.32/1.02/8.13 s): 0.677, 0.471, 0.284, 0.160, 0.110, 0.058, 0.027, 0.0072, 0.0018. Slope of ln h on ln age: -0.61 (0-10 s), -0.86 (10-60 s), -0.92 (beyond). The fitted hazard peaks at 0.79 s.
- Human, the _no_call entry (8,769 gaps, 2.73/68.1/722 s, 7.0 % at the 1,200 s cap): 0.039, 0.022, 0.040, 0.0065, 0.0066, 0.0086, 0.0091, 0.0044, 0.0011. The rise from 1-2 s to 2-4 s is significant (ratio 1.82, z 7.1). The fitted hazard peaks at 0.13 s and misses both the bump and the flat stretch.

Whole trace (12,002 trees, 1,208,163 gaps):
- Tool (0.41/1.69/16.8 s, as the stats file says): 0.434, 0.357, 0.237, 0.135, 0.090, 0.053, 0.021, 0.0070, 0.0018.
- Human (3.08/96.4/1,039 s): 0.038, 0.028, 0.031, 0.0078, 0.0051, 0.0054, 0.0066, 0.0039, 0.0011, with a small rise from 10-20 s to 20-60 s (z 9.6).

F(x|s) for the tool class is at its maximum within 0.25 s of the turn's end for x = 1 to 6 s (F(4|0) = 0.82).
findings.method: scripts/extract_trace.py streams freeinference_16w.programs.jsonl.gz once. scripts/hint_shapes.py rebuilds the samples as replay_programs.py hints_for does with --hint-key command --hint-no-call (the sample of reply k-1's key is the wait of request k of the same stream, x1, capped at 1,200 s). Hazard per bin is -ln(1 - events/at risk)/width, a capped gap counted as censored. The fit is next_turn_policy.GapDistribution.from_quantiles, imported by path, on the client's p10/p50/p90 of ln gap. Tables: out/hint_shapes_A.txt, hint_shapes_B.txt.
findings.implication: Supports the draft's 3.3 statement that both FreeInference entries have falling hazards, so the threshold form F(x|s) >= q must not be used on them. One correction: the human entry is not monotone. It is flat at 0.007-0.009 per s from 4 to 60 s, which gives a 3 % chance of return per 4 s read window at any idle age in that range, too little for an early read to pay.

findings.question: 1b. Per key: what share of returning requests have a key whose hazard rises somewhere in the range of a read time (1-6 s)? How sharp are the sharpest keys, and how often does a session end, by key?
findings.answer:
Replayed population, 82 keys with 100 or more gaps (89.7 % of gaps).

Where the hazard peaks:
- Empirical hazard highest in 0-1 s for 46.8 % of requests, in 1-2 s for 37.9 %, 2-4 s for 13.1 % (8.5 points are _no_call), 4-6 s for 1.6 %, 6-10 s for 0.5 %, never later.
- Trend over 0-10 s: falling for 90.4 %, rising 4.5 %, flat 5.1 %. Over 10-60 s: falling 68.1 %, flat 12.8 %, rising 0 (19.1 % too few gaps).
- A significant rise between adjacent bins from 1 s on: 33.8 % (20 keys). Most are mixtures of harnesses (bash/cat, bash/grep, bash/sed: 1.2 per s in the first second, 0.2 at 1-2 s, 0.3-0.6 at 2-4 s) whose hazard stays below its first-second level.
- Fitted hazard peaks after 1 s for 40.5 %, after 2 s for 6.0 %, after 4 s for 1.9 %, after 6 s for 1.2 % (whole trace: 38.9/12.9/3.9/2.0 %).
- The quantity the threshold rule needs: F(4|s) exceeds F(4|0) by more than 0.05 for 4.8 % of requests (by more than 0.15 for 1.4 %); F(2|s) for 17.6 % (2.8 %); F(6|s) for 2.6 % (0.9 %).

Sharpness (p90/p10):
- Over keys: min 2.3, p10 7.5, median 18.7, p90 35.3.
- The only key under 5 is "other" (0.51/0.63/1.19 s, 7 % of requests), shorter than a read.
- Sharp inside the read range: terminal/ps 1.23/4.19/6.96 s, web_search 2.20/5.61/15.9 s, terminal/tail, computer_use, browser_navigate, about 1-3 % of requests.
- Per agent system (as the replay's table keys them), 16.4 % of requests have p90/p10 under 3, but with medians of 0.3-1.1 s (eval:swe-bench). The hermes+glm-5-turbo terminal keys (about 1.8/3.2/5.4 s, F(4|s) rising from 0.64-0.72 to 0.91-0.98) are 0.9 %.

Stream ends after a reply: 3.6 % of all replies; tool keys 1.5 %; _no_call 22.0 % (12.3 % in the whole trace); bash/echo 27.4 % (the swe-bench submit); other 6.4 %; median key 0.7 %, p90 2.1 %.
findings.method: scripts/hint_shapes.py and hint_shapes_report.py: per key the client's entry quantiles, the engine's fit, bin hazards with a z-test on ln ratios of adjacent bins (variance 1/events), empirical and fitted F(x|s) on a grid of s. Populations A (replayed), A_sys (per system and key), B (whole trace): out/hint_shapes_A.txt, hint_shapes_A_sys.txt, hint_shapes_B.txt. Ends are the last request of each stream by its reply key.
findings.implication: A rule that waits for a rising hazard can apply to 1-5 % of returning requests on this trace. The end signal is concentrated in two keys (_no_call, bash/echo), so a per-key end probability carries most of what an explicit end hint does.

findings.question: 1c. What did the entries the client actually sent look like, for the requests that needed a read?
findings.answer:
Campaign 34 ec_full (15,990 entries; 77/12/11 % answered at key/tool/any level):
- p90/p10 median 13.6 over all entries and 26.0 for the 2,209 readers; 11.0 % of readers under 5.
- 81.8 % of readers' entries have a falling tail (sigma_high >= 1).
- Fitted F(4|s) rises more than 0.15 above F(4|0) for 5.4 % of readers.
- True gap inside p10-p90 for 72.5 % of all and 65.6 % of readers; above the p90 for 28.2 % of readers.
- In minutes 0-70, 72-80 % of readers' entries are the no-call entry.

Campaign 26 nofc_noend (LMCache 262K trace, x10 gaps; 11,733 entries, 96 % at key level):
- p90/p10 median 3.7 (7.0 for readers).
- The fitted hazard peaks after 6 s for 89.5 % of readers.
- F(4|s) rises more than 0.15 for 85.5 % of readers.
findings.method: scripts/hints_sent.py on each client record's hint (p10/p50/p90, matched level) joined to the next request, with readers taken from the server log (a landed read before admission); out/hints_sent.txt.
findings.implication: The falling-hazard regime is a property of FreeInference at x1, not of every setting the paper reports. Campaign 26's hints were sharp, so the draft's sentence that early reads paid only with exact hints there because the hazard falls does not fit that trace. The paper should name which setting exercises the rising-hazard case.

findings.question: 2a. Trace level: with the engine's read_start and the draft's cost with weight c, what is the optimal start per key and the expected gain over reading at arrival, in seconds of TTFT per returning request, and what is the exact-gap ceiling?
findings.answer:
The cost depends on r and W only through x = (r - W)+ and on c and lambda only through lambda L / c. All figures are per returning request whose history is out of memory at the turn's end, with capped gaps treated as censored.

Cells that give nothing:
- W >= r (6 of the 12 cells: (2,2), (2,5), (2,15), (4,5), (4,15), (6,15)): 0.
- c = 0: 0 for any lambda.

c = 1:
| x (s) | cells (r,W) | oracle (s) | rule net, lambda 0 / 1e-6 / 2e-5 / 1e-4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | (6,5) | 0.80 | +0.76 / +0.61 / +0.15 / +0.02 |
| 2 | (2,0), (4,2) | 1.24 | +1.16 / +0.94 / +0.44 / +0.04 |
| 4 | (4,0), (6,2) | 1.82 | +1.66 / +1.31 / +0.80 / +0.20 |
| 6 | (6,0) | 2.25 | +2.01 / +1.52 / +1.05 / +0.41 |

At x = 2 the rule says "now" for 89 %, 71 % and 10 % of requests at lambda = 1e-6, 2e-5, 1e-4.

c = 0.3: x = 2: +0.35 / +0.25 / +0.03 / -0.00; x = 4: +0.50 / +0.36 / +0.10 / +0.01.

Where the per-key optimum sits: at 0 (read now, the same as keeping) or at arrival for almost every key. A timed start adds 0.001-0.024 s in sample over the better end and loses out of sample (-0.002 to -0.004 s at 1e-6, -0.17 to -0.36 s at 2e-5). Real timing gains: web_search (start 0.7 s, +0.02 s per request of the key out of sample) and clarify (+0.06 s), 0.7 % of requests, +0.0002 s per returning request overall. Whole trace: the same (12-15 keys, 0.3 % of requests, +0.0004 to +0.0016 s).

Other policies:
- The best static start per key without a release nets less than the rule (x = 4, 2e-5: +0.48 in sample, +0.09 out of sample, against +0.80).
- Just-in-time on the p10 nets +1.44 at 1e-6 and -2.7 at 2e-5 (x = 4).
findings.method: scripts/fetch_value.py with next_turn_policy.py imported by path. Per entry (own key from 5 gaps, else tool, else any): read_start on the 64-point support with rent = lambda x median history tokens / c, scored on the key's true gaps, with the pin given back as ec_release does (5 s after fewer than 4 support points remain) and a later turn counted as reading at arrival. "emp" is the best start on the key's own gaps, in sample and with a 2-fold split (fixed seed). The vectorized start rule was checked against read_start on 5,000 random cases (0 mismatches) and reproduces the review's check (start 127.4 s; 1.81 s against 1.10 s). Tables: out/fetch_value_A_censored.txt (grid, where the optimum sits, per-key starts), fetch_value_B_censored.txt.
findings.implication: The draft's claim holds on this trace: before arrival there is no timing decision, only keep-or-drop, and the part of the engine's rule that earns its net is the release of the pin, which is a holding-time decision that belongs to Retain. A Fetch-before-arrival rule is not worth new engine work for FreeInference; expected gain from timing is 0.000-0.002 s per returning request.

findings.question: 2b. How much is left once the prefix has been out of memory for a while, which is when reads actually happen?
findings.answer:
Who reads: in campaign 34's minutes 0-70 the readers are long-gap requests. Median gap 49-66 s (ec_full) and 163-490 s (jit_exact); 79-98 % of requests with a gap of 60 s or more read, against 0-5 % of those under 10 s. In minutes 70-110 the median reader gap is 8-10 s.

Rule net by eviction age (x = 4, c = 1, lambda = 1e-6 / 2e-5 / 1e-4), per request returning later than that age:
| out of memory for | share of returning requests | rule net (s) | oracle (s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 s | 37.0 % | +1.40 / +0.52 / +0.03 | 2.73 |
| 10 s | 14.8 % | +0.59 / +0.015 / +0.002 | 3.70 |
| 60 s | 6.0 % | +0.04 / +0.002 / 0.000 | 3.88 |
| 300 s | 1.8 % | +0.004 / 0 / 0 | 3.95 |

At x = 2 and 10 s: +0.25 / +0.002 / +0.001 of 1.92.

In-sample timed starts at these ages (+0.02 to +0.19 s) are starts hundreds of seconds out at the last gaps of the tail and lose out of sample.
findings.method: The same script, with the gap distribution conditioned on idle age a (remaining_gaps for the fit, gaps > a for the truth). Reader shares by gap come from the per-request tables of campaign 34 (scripts/read_table.py).
findings.implication: For the reads that occur at light and moderate load (gaps of tens of seconds to minutes) a distribution hint recovers at most 16 % of the exact-hint ceiling at lambda = 1e-6 and under 0.5 % at 2e-5 or more. Reading back before arrival is empty there; what is left belongs to the eviction order.

findings.question: 2c. On the runs: what is the most a read before arrival could have saved per regime, and does it match what exact hints measured?
findings.answer:
Ceiling = min(gap, stall) per returning request, where stall = admission minus the turn's GPU turn. "c-weighted" multiplies by the share of the stall with no other ready turn waiting.

Campaign 34:
| minutes | readers | measured c | ceiling (s) | c-weighted (s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0-30 | 0.4-2.6 % | 0.82-0.92 | 0.000-0.017 | up to 0.014 |
| 30-70 | 4-9 % (16 % jit_p50) | 0.002-0.066 | 0.003-0.023 (0.33 jit_p50) | at most 0.002 |
| 70-110 | 23-27 % | 0.000 | 1.97-2.11 (3.96 jit_p50) | 0.000-0.001 |

The 70-110 figure assumes an unchanged read line. Stall there is 4.7-4.9 s per returning request.

Campaign 33 (TraceLab, never saturates): readers 0.4 %, ceiling 0.003 s.

Campaign 26 (Triton, 44 users, 70 GB, x10 gaps; c 0.44-0.99 by 10-minute window, 0.71 weighted by stall):
- Stall per returning request: 0.319 s (nofc_noend), 0.251 s (nofc), 0.159 s (ec_r13), 0.098 s (jit_exact_d).
- The differences to the exact-hint arm, 0.15-0.22 s, match the record's 0.16-0.20 s.
- Ceiling 0.225-0.288 s (0.159-0.216 s c-weighted).
- read_start on the entries sent, given the true x, would save 0.25 / 0.16 / 0.12 / 0.09 s at lambda = 1e-6 / 2e-5 / 5e-5 / 1e-4, a net of +0.21 / +0.10 / +0.06 / +0.02 s at c = 1.
findings.method: scripts/extract_run.py (server.log events plus the ReqTimeStats lines, which give every request's queue entry and queue duration), runlib.py (queue rebuilt in arrival order; positions match the logged ntp_arrive position exactly for 14,985 of 15,306 turns and within 1 for the rest), read_table.py and ceiling.py. A turn's GPU turn is the first time admission took a later arrival while it waited on its read; when the pool had room (usage under 0.90) it is the first time no ready turn was ahead of it. Tables: out/ceiling.txt, out/regimes_*.txt.
findings.implication: On FA3 with FreeInference there is nothing for a pre-arrival read to win: 0.02 s at most where c is high, 0.000 s weighted by c once the queue persists. The paper's pre-arrival case needs campaign 26's kind of setting (sharp gaps, light load, reads present), where the prize is 0.2-0.3 s and is bounded by room, not by the hint.

findings.question: 3a. How wrong is the engine's predicted admission at each decision, by regime and by queue position?
findings.answer:
Error e = GPU turn minus prediction, ec_full / jit_exact.

At arrival, (position + 0.5) / rate, planned turns:
| regime | median (s) | p5 (s) | p95 (s) | other |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| minutes 0-30 | 0.00 | | | |e| p90 0.6 / 0.5 |
| pool < 0.90 | | | | |e| p90 0.47 / 0.03 |
| minutes 30-70 | 0.00 / 0.00 | -4.3 / -3.7 | +5.0 / +4.6 | p20 -1.7 / -1.4, p80 +1.9 / +1.8, sd 2.9 / 2.6 |
| minutes 70-90 | -1.1 / -0.6 | -9.4 / -8.8 | +6.1 / +8.4 | |
| minutes 90-110 | -8.8 / -10.2 | -18.8 / -18.5 | +5.0 / +0.6 | |

By position at arrival (minutes 30-110):
- 2-5: |e| p90 1.6 / 1.3 s.
- 6-15: 2.6 / 2.7 s.
- 16-30: 5.2 / 4.6 s.
- 31-50: median -1.4 / -1.2 s, |e| p90 7.7 / 8.0 s.
- 51 and over: median -9.0 / -10.3 s, |e| p90 17 s.
- Relative error e / prediction: median -0.11, p5 -0.53, p95 +0.6.

The late bias is pass-over: in minutes 90-110, 51 % of the turns ahead of an arriving turn (30 of 59 at the median) are waiting on their own reads. Counting only the ready ones errs the other way (+4.6 / +3.8 s median); the mean of the two is within -2.3 / -3.1 s.

Readers' admission against max(arrival + position/rate, own landing) + 0.4 s: median -0.03 / +0.01 s, |e| p50 0.40 / 0.38 s, p90 3.3 / 2.9 s. Against position/rate alone the median is +8.5 / +13.0 s.

At the first hold (ntp_hold), minutes 30-70: median -0.37 / -0.26 s, p5 -5.0 / -5.7 s, p95 +6.5 / +6.1 s.

At the replayed release, minutes 30-70: p5 -3.8 / -2.2 s, p20 -1.4 / -1.1 s, p50 -0.16 / -0.03 s, p80 +1.7 / +1.8 s, p95 +4.5 / +3.7 s. Minutes 70-90: p50 -1.25 / -0.75 s, p5 -9.4 / -9.8 s. Minutes 90-110: p50 -8.3 / -9.5 s.
findings.method: scripts/f1_landing.py sections A1-A3 on campaign 34 ec_full and jit_exact (also run on ec_exact and jit_p50, which agree). Predictions come from ntp_admit pred_wait_ql_ms, ntp_hold wait_ms, and the rebuilt (position + 0.5) / rate at the replayed release. The hold replay reproduces the engine's inputs at the logged first hold (predicted wait and load: median difference 0.00 s) and releases within 0.1 s of the actual dispatch for reads that did not wait in the line. Estimator comparison in scripts/d_estimators.py. Tables: out/f1_landing_c34_*.txt, out/d_estimators.txt.
findings.implication: The draft's estimate of D (median error 0.4-0.5 s) is confirmed for readers once their landing is known, and the queue part is unbiased while the SSD keeps up. Its spread at the release (sd 2.1-2.5 s, p20 about -1.3 s) is what a landing quantile would use. In the SSD-saturated phase the estimate is 9-10 s long, but the hold does not bind there (0-17 holds), so fixing it changes no release; it would matter only to a pre-arrival W.

findings.question: 3b. Replaying the release rule with other margins (own read time fixed): what is the stall and pin trade-off, and where does today's fixed 2 s sit?
findings.answer:
Reads held by today's rule over the whole run: 818 (ec_full), 710 (jit_exact), 819 (ec_exact), 254 (jit_p50), mean 22-23K tokens. The replay at 2 s reproduces the actual means (stall 0.81 against 0.84 s, pin 2.65 against 2.65 s in ec_full).

Trade-off for held reads, ec_full / jit_exact:
| margin (s) | late % | stall s per read | pin K token-s per read |
|---|---|---|---|
| -2 | 81 / 82 | 3.22 / 3.99 | 11.8 / 7.4 |
| 0 | 55 / 54 | 1.84 / 2.74 | 30.8 / 27.9 |
| +1 | 34 / 35 | 1.21 / 2.05 | 48.0 / 45.6 |
| +2 (today) | 21.5 / 22.7 | 0.81 / 1.46 | 66.3 / 64.3 |
| +3 | 16.5 / 18.7 | 0.68 / 1.27 | 91.5 / 86.4 |
| +4 | 12.7 / 14.9 | 0.59 / 1.15 | 118 / 111 |
| +6 | 9.5 / 12.8 | 0.49 / 1.06 | 161 / 149 |
| release at park | 7.2 / 9.7 | 0.42 / 0.93 | 202 / 213 |

The 7-10 % still late at release-at-park are the line and the read-time error, not the margin.

Margins from the error quantiles, q = 0.05 / 0.2 / 0.5 / 0.8 / 0.95:
- ec_full: +5.2 / +1.9 / +0.3 / -1.7 / -4.1 s.
- jit_exact: +6.1 / +1.85 / +0.3 / -1.5 / -4.3 s.
- So today's 2 s is the q = 0.20 point in all four arms (+1.94, +1.85, +1.60, +2.07 s).

Exchange rate around 2 s: 0.4-0.6 s of stall per 18-19K token-seconds going from 1 to 2 s (2.2e-5 to 3.1e-5 s per token-second), and 0.13-0.20 s per 22-25K going from 2 to 3 s (5e-6 to 9e-6).

By window for all reads (ec_full):
- Minutes 30-70 (625 reads, 423 held): 21 % late, 0.27 s stall, 2.63 s pin (68K token-s) at 2 s; 49 % late, 0.93 s, 34K at 0; 16 % late, 0.24 s, 105K at 4.
- Minutes 70-90: 61 % late and 6.35 s stall at 2 s; 6.16 s at release-at-park.
- Minutes 90-110: 100 % late at every margin (17 holds).
- Pool under 0.90: no read held in any arm, so the margin does nothing.

Campaign 26 nofc_noend: 122 of 2,381 reads held; there 2 s is about the q = 0.45 point (q = 0.2 is +7 s).
findings.method: scripts/f1_landing.py section B. runlib.hold_replay recomputes, on a 0.1 s grid with the line as it was (parked and in-flight reads from the log, the read thread's ms/page EWMA rebuilt from s2h_io), each read's position, (position + 0.5) / rate and the pages ahead in deadline order, and releases when wait - load <= margin (never held at positions 0-1). Landing moves with the release; stall = (landing + 0.4 s - GPU turn)+, pin = (GPU turn - landing)+ times the read's tokens. Tables: out/f1_landing_c34_ec_full.txt, _jit_exact.txt, _ec_exact.txt, _jit_p50.txt, f1_landing_c26_nofc_noend.txt.
findings.implication: The fixed 2 s is not arbitrary in effect: it lands held reads at the 20th percentile of the due time. What a quantile rule can move is bounded by this curve: at most 0.4-0.5 s of a held reader's own stall (release at park) or 60K token-seconds per held read (land at the last moment), on 5 % of requests.

findings.question: 3c. Which q would q = lambda L / (c + lambda L) pick per regime, what changes against today, and is the 2 s margin already near the optimum?
findings.answer:
Measured c (share of stall seconds with no other ready turn waiting), ec_full / jit_exact / ec_exact / jit_p50:
| minutes | c | host-pool state |
|---|---|---|
| 0-30 | 0.83 / 0.91 / 0.88 / 0.89 | pool under 0.90 on 34-100 % of batch lines with a queue |
| 30-70 | 0.057 / 0.019 / 0.061 / 0.005 | ready turns waiting 99 % of the time |
| 70-110 | 0.000 | |

Minutes 0-30: q = 0.002 to 0.63 for lambda 1e-7 to 1e-4, but only 3-9 reads are held, so the change is 0.000 s.

Minutes 30-70 (L about 20K tokens), ec_full / jit_exact:
| lambda | q | margin (s) | stall per read (s) | regime mean TTFT, readers' own (s) | c-weighted (s) | pinned tokens |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1e-7 | 0.04 / 0.10 | +5.2 / +1.8 | -0.04 / +0.09 | -0.005 / +0.005 | within 0.0003 | 17.7K to 31.3K / 8.9K to 8.3K |
| 1e-6 | 0.27 / 0.52 | +1.2 / 0.0 | +0.20 / +0.56 | +0.02 / +0.03 | about +0.001 | -3.2K / -4.8K |
| 2e-5 | 0.88 / 0.96 | -3.0 / -4.0 | +1.7 / +1.4 | +0.19 / +0.08 | +0.011 / +0.002 | -15.1K / -8.5K (-0.9 / -0.5 % of the host pool) |
| 1e-4 | 0.97 / 0.99 | | +2.0 / +1.6 | +0.23 / +0.09 | | 17.7K to 1.4K / 8.9K to 0.4K |

Minutes 70-90: c = 0 gives q = 1 for any lambda > 0. Margin -13 to -15 s, +6.9 to +8.9 s for each read (+1.7 to +2.0 s on the regime's mean counted on readers, 0.000 c-weighted), pinned -21K to -23K tokens (-1.3 to -1.4 %).

Near the optimum? On ec_full's held reads the cost-minimizing margin is +1.75 s at (c = 1, lambda = 2e-5), where today costs 2.135 against 2.115 s per read, and +1.75 s at (c = 0.05, lambda = 1e-6), 0.107 against 0.106. So 2 s is within 1-4 % of the best wherever lambda/c is about 2e-5. Off that line the best margin is release at park (lambda/c <= 1e-6) or -6 to -12 s (lambda/c >= 4e-4).

Plausible lambda: campaign 26's 70 to 100 GB step (305K tokens for 0.52 s at 1.63 requests per s) gives 2.8e-6 s per token-second on average, and about 1.2e-5 at the tight end if reads halve per 5 GB. For campaign 34 at 160 GB there is no measurement.

Two defects of the rule as written:
- The quantile of the admission error alone picks 1.3 s where the cost optimum is 1.75 s (c = 1, lambda = 2e-5), because the read-time error also moves the landing.
- With c measured where the hold binds, q goes to 1 and every held reader lands late.
findings.method: scripts/f1_landing.py section C and scripts/f1_summary.py (out/f1_summary.txt): c from runlib.ready_series (queued turns with no read parked or in flight) over each stall interval; q from lambda x median read tokens; the margin is minus the q-quantile of the error at the replayed release; outcomes from the margin replay; pinned tokens on average = pin token-seconds over the window length. The lambda range is derived from campaign26/DECISIONS.md (30 GB bought 0.52 s; reads halve per 5 GB).
findings.implication: F1 is not worth building as a TTFT lever. Expected change in campaign 34: at most 0.013 s of mean TTFT weighted by c in either direction, and about 1 % of the host pool (16K tokens) freed at the price of 1.4-8.9 s more wait for each held reader. In campaign 26's light-load setting a larger margin would save up to 1.7 s on each of 122 held reads, about 0.02 s per returning request. If it is built anyway: use the quantile of the landing error (admission and read time together), and bound q so that c near 0 does not turn the hold into late-on-purpose.

findings.question: 4a. How long did reads wait between release and dispatch, and between dispatch and landing, by regime?
findings.answer:
Reads of queued turns, medians (p90), ec_full / jit_exact.

| minutes | hold (park to release) | line (release to dispatch) | thread FIFO | own I/O | I/O end to usable | release to usable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0-30 | 0 s | 0.00 s | 0.00 s | 0.62 / 0.39 s | 0.01 s | 0.70 / 0.45 s |
| 30-70 | 1.9 / 5.1 s (422 / 270 held) | 0.09 / 0.09 s (p90 4.8 / 2.8, mean 1.4 / 0.9) | 0.00 s | 0.94 / 0.85 s | | 1.70 / 1.23 s (p90 6.9 / 4.8) |
| 70-90 | | 11.9 / 11.0 s (p90 29.9 / 32.5) | 1.0 / 0.9 s | 1.34 / 1.27 s | | 14.2 / 13.2 s |
| 90-110 | | 42.0 / 44.4 s (p90 50.7 / 53.6) | 1.33 / 1.35 s | 1.34 / 1.40 s | | 44.7 / 47.4 s |

Minutes 0-30 are the same with the pool under 0.90. In minutes 90-110, 29-30 % of reads were dispatched only once their turn reached positions 0-1.

jit_p50's early reads move the line 20 minutes earlier: line 3.8 s in minutes 30-70, 51 s in 70-90, 66 s in 90-110.

Write hold: 28-30 holds a run, 57-81 s in total, median 2.0-2.8 s. It overlaps the line wait of 12-19 % of reads in minutes 70-110 and adds 0.26-0.45 s on average.
findings.method: scripts/f3_line.py section A: srs_park, the replayed release, srs_dispatch, s2h_io (end and ms) and srs_pin per read, paired per rid in time order (in-flight pages rebuilt from these match the logged inflight_pages at 96-97 % of dispatches); write hold from srs_write_hold. Tables: out/f3_line_c34_*.txt, out/regimes_c34_*.txt.
findings.implication: Until minute 70 a read is its own I/O (about 1 s for 20K tokens) plus a line of 0.1 s; after it the line is 85-95 % of the read time. The write hold is a small part of it, so a read-time estimate needs the parked pages, not a model of the write hold.

findings.question: 4b. How wrong was the read time the planner used before arrival and at the hold, and what would an estimate that counts parked reads ahead (by deadline) and the write hold have predicted?
findings.answer:
Before arrival (ec_full's last ec_start before each reading turn; planned read without its 1 s margin, against release to usable):
| minutes | planned (s) | actual (s) | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0-30 | 2.09 | 1.07 | 0.49 |
| 30-70 | 3.25 | 1.99 | 0.56 |
| 70-90 | 5.52 | 14.9 | 2.8 |
| 90-110 | 6.05 | 46.6 | 7.5 |

Planned W against arrival to GPU turn: 7.3 against 9.4 s, 15.7 against 15.0 s, 27.6 against 19.1 s (minutes 30-70, 70-90, 90-110). "Read longer than W" by plan: 15 %, 1 %, 0 %; in fact 6 %, 51 %, 100 %.

Staged reads of jit_p50: planned 5.8 / 9.4 / 8.2 s against 8.3 / 49.5 / 67.5 s.

The same planner formula (own pages plus pages in flight) evaluated when the read was parked: 2.4 s against 1.7 s (minutes 30-70), 5.2 s against 14-16 s (median error +9.2 s), 5.9 s against 44.8 s (+38.6 s).

The hold's estimate (plus parked reads ordered ahead by deadline):
- Minutes 70-90: ratio actual/estimate 0.89-0.93, median |error| 1.8-2.5 s, p90 7.6-9.5 s.
- Minutes 90-110: ratio 1.00-1.01, median |error| 3.4-3.5 s, p90 10-11 s.
- With an empty line it is about 1 s too long, like the planner's (2.9 against 1.7 s).

Adding the write hold (the rest of a hold that is on) or counting in arrival order changes these by under 0.1 s.

The 1 s excess is the fixed lags: the engine adds 0.904 s (0.5 allocation, 0.044, 0.36 drain), but an uncontended read measures 0.049 s + 2.84 ms per page (0.0444 ms per token; 399 reads; non-I/O part median 0.013 s).
findings.method: scripts/f3_line.py sections B and C: estimates recomputed from the replayed line state with the engine's L3LoadModel constants and the EWMA rebuilt from s2h_io; ec_start read_ms and wait_ms and ntp_due case 1 load_ms from the logs; actual = release (replayed) to srs_pin. The uncontended fit is an OLS of release-to-usable on pages over reads with nothing in flight and no hold, across the four campaign 34 arms.
findings.implication: The estimate F3 asks for already exists in the engine (read_not_before's pages ahead) and is accurate to a few seconds where the pre-arrival one is 3-7 times short. The calibration worth doing is the opposite end: replace the 0.9 s lag seeds with measured lags. They make the hold's effective margin about 3 s (measured pin of readers that landed early: median 2.4-2.6 s) and overstate x by about 1 s at light load, the one regime where c is near 1. Measured, an uncontended FA3 read (0.05 s + 0.0444 ms per token) ties recompute (0.037-0.044 ms per token); the draft's "plus 0.9 s of lags" in section 2 is the seed, not the measurement.

findings.question: F3 and F2 together: what would the expected-cost start do in campaign 34 if it were given the true read time?
findings.answer:
Today the rule sees r below W and says "arrival" for every turn of the saturated phase (ec_full: 548 of 550 decisions in minutes 70-90, 597 of 597 in 90-110, 1 read staged in the run).

Given the true exposed read time and today's stall weight of 1, read_start on the entries sent says "now" for 52 % of the 1,153 stalled readers of minutes 70-110 at the campaign's price 5e-5 (60 % at 2e-5, 45 % at 1e-4). That is about 600 early reads into a read thread that is already 100 % busy. The rule's own accounting credits 0.42 s per returning request; weighted by the measured c it is 0.000 s, and net of pins it is -0.12 s.

The single read ec_full did stage (at 1,198.5 s idle) is an artifact of the two 1,200 s caps: its "wait" targets always summed to 1,200 s, and on the trace a start at 1,196 s is the in-sample optimum for the no-call entry only because 7 % of human gaps sit exactly at the cap.
findings.method: scripts/ceiling.py (rule rows): read_start per stalled reader with x = its measured stall, the entry the client sent, rent = lambda x the read's tokens, scored on its true gap, by window; c from the ready-turn series. The ec_start and ntp_stage lines of rid ec_full-c100-t3 in the ec_full server log. The replay-mode table (out/fetch_value_A_replay.txt) shows the cap optimum.
findings.implication: F3 must not ship alone. A correct read time before arrival makes the expected-cost arm an early reader exactly when the SSD is the bottleneck, which is what cost jit_p50 its 0.6-0.7 s. F2 (c measured, 0.000 there) cancels it. Ship F2 first or together with F3, and take the cap mass out of the support (or cap the client and the engine differently) before reading anything into staged reads near 1,200 s.

surprises: The hold binds only where lateness is free. No read was held with the pool under 0.90 in any of the four campaign 34 arms, and where reads were held the measured c is 0.005-0.06 (minutes 30-70) or 0.000 (later). So a quantile q = lambda L / (c + lambda L) evaluated at the release goes to 1 for any lambda of 2e-5 or more and would land every held read 3-13 s after its turn.

Today's fixed 2 s margin is the 20th percentile of the measured admission error on held reads in all four campaign 34 arms (+1.6 to +2.1 s), and cost-optimal within 1-4 % along lambda/c of about 2e-5. On Triton (campaign 26) the same 2 s is only about the 45th percentile.

The engine's read-time estimate carries 0.904 s of fixed lag seeds; the measured non-I/O part of an uncontended read is 0.05 s (median 0.013 s). The estimate is therefore twice too long with an empty line and the hold's effective margin is about 3 s. An uncontended FA3 read (0.05 s + 0.0444 ms per token) ties recompute (0.037-0.044 ms per token).

In the SSD-saturated phase 51 % of the turns ahead of an arriving turn are waiting on their own reads (30 of 59), so position over rate puts the GPU turn 9-10 s too late at the median. Counting only ready turns is 4-5 s too early; the mean of the two is within 2-3 s.

Campaign 26's hints were sharp, not heavy-tailed: p90/p10 median 3.7, hazard still rising within a read time for 86 % of readers' entries (x10 gaps on a SWE-bench-heavy trace). The draft's explanation of campaign 26 by falling hazards does not fit it. There the ceiling was 0.23-0.29 s per returning request and exact hints took 0.15-0.22 s; my stall accounting reproduces the record's 0.16-0.20 s within 0.02 s.

The part of the engine's rule 1 that earns its net on FreeInference is the release of the pin (ec_release), not the start time: read-now-then-release nets +0.80 s per reading request at x = 4 and lambda = 2e-5, against +0.48 s for the best static start per key in sample and +0.09 s out of sample.

Per-key 'interior' optimal starts are overfitting. In sample they sit 100-1,000 s out at the last gaps of the tail and add 0.001-0.024 s; chosen on half the gaps and scored on the other half they lose 0.2-1.9 s per reading request at lambda of 2e-5 or more. Only web_search and clarify (0.7 % of requests) show a real timing gain.

The 1,200 s gap cap is exploitable and the engine exploits it: 7 % of human gaps sit exactly at the cap, a start at 1,196 s is the in-sample optimum for the no-call entry (+0.28 s per no-call request in replay mode), and ec_full's single staged read (at 1,198.5 s idle) is that.

Several of the most frequent keys are two populations mixed across harnesses (bash/cat, bash/grep, bash/sed: hazard 1.2 per s in the first second, 0.2 at 1-2 s, 0.3-0.6 at 2-4 s). Per-system entries separate them, which is why 16 % of requests have per-system p90/p10 under 3 while the pooled keys do not.

ec_exact's 0.3-0.4 s lead over ec_full and jit_exact in campaign 34 is not early reads: it staged 39 reads in the run, and the pre-arrival ceiling weighted by c is 0.000-0.004 s. Whatever it is, it comes from which prefixes stay in memory (readers 6.0 % against 9.4 % in minutes 30-70), not from read timing.
